notes.32:14: Vulgate tenebrae et palpatio ("darkness and groping") interprets Hebrew ophel wa-bachan ("hill/citadel and watchtower") through roots meaning "darkness" and "testing/feeling."
notes.32:15: The Vulgate retains the Hebrew word carmel untranslated here and in verse 16; besides referring to Mount Carmel, the term means a fertile orchard or garden land.
notes.32:18: Vulgate in pulchritudine pacis ("in the beauty of peace") derives Hebrew naweh ("dwelling/abode") from the root meaning "to be beautiful."
notes.33:3: Vulgate "A voce angeli" ("At the voice of the angel") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("at the sound of tumult"), reflecting an interpretive tradition linking this verse to the angel who struck the Assyrian camp (cf. Isa 37:36).
notes.33:7: Vulgate "videntes" ("the seers" or "those who see") renders a rare Hebrew term usually taken as "valiant ones" or "heroes," deriving it from the verb "to see"; "angeli pacis" literally means "angels/messengers of peace."
notes.33:11: Vulgate "Concipietis ardorem" ("You will conceive heat") contrasts with the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "chaff" or "dry grass" parallel to "stubble."
notes.33:14: Vulgate "de vobis" and "ex vobis" ("among you") address the sinners in Zion directly, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "among us," placing the questions in the mouths of the terrified sinners.
notes.33:18: Vulgate "legis verba ponderans" ("weighing the words of the law") and "doctor parvulorum" ("teacher of little children") are distinctive Latin renderings of Hebrew expressions referring to one who weighs (the tribute) and one who counts the towers.
notes.34:5: The Vulgate uses the Greco-Latin geographical name "Idumæa" ("Idumea") here and "Edom" in 34:6, whereas the Hebrew text uses "Edom" in both verses.
notes.34:6: Vulgate "de sanguine medullatorum arietum" ("from the blood of rams full of marrow") diverges from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "from the fat of the kidneys of rams."
notes.34:7: Vulgate "unicornes" ("unicorns"), following the Septuagint "monokerotes," renders Hebrew "re'emim" (wild oxen).
notes.34:14: Vulgate "dæmonia" ("demons"), "onocentauris" ("onocentaurs," mythical half-human, half-donkey creatures), "pilosus" ("the hairy one"), and "lamia" ("the lamia," a mythical night-monster) follow Septuagint and classical Latin equivalents for Hebrew desert-creature and night-spirit terms; similarly, "draconum" ("dragons") in 34:13 and 35:7 renders Hebrew "tannim" (jackals).
notes.34:16: Vulgate "quod ex ore meo procedit, ille mandavit" ("what proceeds from my mouth, He has commanded") distinguishes the prophet's spoken message ("my mouth") from the Lord ("He") who commanded it, smoothing a grammatical shift in the Hebrew text ("My mouth has commanded").
notes.35:4: Vulgate "ultionem adducet retributionis" ("will bring the vengeance of retribution") links the two nouns in a genitive phrase governed by "will bring," whereas the Hebrew text places "vengeance" and "recompense of God" in parallel clauses.
notes.35:6: Vulgate "aperta erit" ("will be opened") parallels "will be opened" in 35:5, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "will shout for joy" or "will sing."
notes.35:8: Vulgate "et hæc erit vobis directa via" ("and this will be a straight way for you") gives a clear sense to a difficult Hebrew clause (literally "and it is for them; one walking the way").
notes.36:5: The Vulgate asks with what counsel or strength Hezekiah plans to rebel (quo consilio vel fortitudine rebellare disponis) and states that he has withdrawn (recessisti) from Sennacherib, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text says counsel and strength for war are mere words of the lips and asks why he has rebelled.
notes.36:8: Latin trade te ("surrender yourself") reflects the Vulgate's rendering of the Hebrew idiom for making a pledge or wager, and the closing clause (nec poteris) is framed as a negative statement rather than a conditional ("if you are able").
notes.36:16: Latin Facite mecum benedictionem ("Make a blessing with me") translates the Hebrew idiom literally; in context it means to come to terms or make peace.
notes.36:19: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text (which has plural "gods"), the Vulgate reads singular deus ("god") in the first two questions before shifting to a plural verb (liberaverunt, "have they delivered").
notes.37:4: In the Vulgate, exprobrandum ("to revile") is paired with ad blasphemandum ("to blaspheme") as Rabshakeh's act, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text makes the Lord the subject who will rebuke the words He has heard.
notes.37:24: The Vulgate treats the Hebrew common noun karmel ("orchard" or "lush woodland") as a proper name, Carmeli ("its Carmel").
notes.37:25: Latin aggerum ("of the embankments") reflects Jerome's reading of Hebrew masor as ramparts or siege-works rather than a poetic name for Egypt, and exsiccavi uses the past tense ("I dried up").
notes.37:26: Latin in eradicationem collium compugnantium ("for the uprooting of warring hills") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of turning fortified cities into heaps of ruins.
notes.37:30: Latin pomis vescere ("feed on fruit") interprets the rare Hebrew term for second-year volunteer growth as orchard fruit.
notes.38:8: The Vulgate explicitly renders Hebrew ma'alot ("steps/degrees") as horologio ("sundial") and lineis ("lines"), before using gradus ("steps") in the final clause.
notes.38:10: Latin quaesivi ("I have sought") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering where the Masoretic Text reads "I am deprived of / consigned."
notes.38:11: Latin habitatorem quietis ("inhabitant of rest") reflects Jerome's rendering of Hebrew chadel as "rest" or "cessation."
notes.38:14: Latin meditabor ("I will meditate") translates Hebrew hagah by its primary sense of meditating/murmuring rather than "moan" or "coo."
notes.39:2: Latin verbum literally means "word," functioning here as a Hebraism for "thing" (Hebrew davar), parallel to res ("thing") in 39:4.
notes.39:8: Latin locutus est ("He has spoken") is third person referring to the Lord, distinct from the Masoretic Text's second-person "you have spoken."
notes.40:1: The Vulgate pairs passive/middle consolamini with the vocative popule meus ("Take comfort, My people"), whereas the Hebrew has a transitive imperative with "My people" as its object ("Comfort My people").
notes.40:2: Latin malitia ("wickedness") is a Vulgate-distinct reading where the Masoretic Text reads "her warfare" or "hard service."
notes.40:8: The Clementine Vulgate reads Domini nostri ("of our Lord"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "of our God."
notes.40:22: Latin velut nihilum ("like nothing") is a Vulgate-distinct rendering where the Masoretic Text has ka-doq ("like a thin curtain/gauze").
notes.40:23: Latin secretorum scrutatores ("searchers of secrets") reflects Jerome's etymological rendering of Hebrew rozenim ("princes/rulers") via the root for "secret."
notes.40:29: Latin his qui non sunt ("to those who are not") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering where the Masoretic Text reads "to him who has no might."
notes.41:2: The Vulgate reads 'Justum' ('the Righteous One') and 'vocavit eum ut sequeretur se' ('called him to follow Him'), diverging from the Hebrew 'whom righteousness/victory meets at his feet.'
notes.41:4: The Vulgate 'primus et novissimus ego sum' ('I am the first and the last') differs from the Hebrew 'I am the first, and with the last I am He.'
notes.41:7: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew word for 'anvil' as 'tunc temporis' ('at that time'), reading it from the homonym meaning 'time.'
notes.41:10: Distinctive Vulgate readings here include 'ne declines' ('do not turn aside' vs. Hebrew 'do not be dismayed'), perfect-tense verbs ('have strengthened ... have helped ... has upheld'), and 'dextera Justi mei' ('the right hand of My Righteous One' vs. Hebrew 'My righteous right hand').
notes.41:14: The Vulgate reads 'qui mortui estis ex Israel' ('you who are dead from Israel'), vocalizing the Hebrew word for 'men' as 'dead.'
notes.42:2: The Vulgate 'neque accipiet personam' (literally, 'nor will he accept a person,' the biblical idiom for showing partiality) diverges from the Hebrew 'nor lift up [his voice].'
notes.42:4: The Vulgate reads 'Non erit tristis, neque turbulentus' ('He will not be sad nor turbulent'), differing from the Hebrew 'he will not grow faint or be crushed.'
notes.42:11: The Vulgate punctuates 'In domibus habitabit Cedar' ('Kedar will dwell in houses') as a separate clause, whereas the Hebrew links 'the villages where Kedar dwells' to the preceding call; Latin 'Cedar' is rendered with the standard modern English spelling 'Kedar.'
notes.42:14: The Vulgate 'loquar; dissipabo, et absorbebo simul' ('I will speak; I will scatter and swallow up together') diverges from the Hebrew imagery of groaning, gasping, and panting.
notes.42:19: The Vulgate reads 'ad quem nuntios meos misi' ('the one to whom I have sent My messengers') and 'qui venundatus est' ('the one who has been sold'), diverging from the Hebrew 'my messenger whom I send' and 'the one at peace / dedicated one.'
notes.43:3: Latin propitiationem renders Hebrew kopher ("ransom") with a sacrificial term meaning "propitiation" or "atonement"; Latin Aethopiam (for Aethiopiam) and Saba correspond to Ethiopia (Hebrew Cush) and Seba.
notes.43:7: The Vulgate reads the active qui invocat nomen meum ("who calls upon My name"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads a passive ("who is called by My name").
notes.43:14: The Vulgate reads vectes universos ("all the bars," taking the Hebrew term as gate or prison bars rather than "fugitives") and in navibus suis gloriantes ("boasting in their ships").
notes.43:19: Latin nova ("new things") is plural and utique cognoscetis ea is an emphatic affirmation ("surely you will know them"), differing from the singular and rhetorical question in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.44:2: Latin rectissime ("most upright one") translates the Hebrew poetic name Jeshurun by its meaning rather than transliterating it, and the Vulgate punctuates ab utero ("from the womb") with auxiliator tuus ("your helper").
notes.44:8: Latin formator ("fashioner") interprets the underlying Hebrew consonants in the sense of forming or shaping, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "rock."
notes.44:18: Latin obliti sunt is the passive of oblino ("to plaster or smear over"), not obliviscor ("to forget"), portraying the idolaters as coated over so that their eyes cannot see.
notes.44:20: The Vulgate reads Pars ejus cinis est; cor insipiens adoravit illud ("Part of it is ashes; a foolish heart has worshiped it") and Forte ("Perhaps"), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray ... Is there not...?").
notes.44:21: The Vulgate reads an active warning ne obliviscaris mei ("do not forget Me"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads a passive promise ("you will not be forgotten by Me").
notes.45:1: Latin christo meo ("My anointed") agrees with the Septuagint against the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("His anointed"), and dorsa regum vertam ("turn the backs of kings") differs from the Hebrew "ungird the loins of kings."
notes.45:4: Latin assimilavi te (literally "I have likened you") is Jerome's rendering of the Hebrew verb for giving an honorary title or surname.
notes.45:7: Latin malum ("evil"), contrasted here with pacem ("peace"), refers to calamity, adversity, or physical hardship rather than moral evil.
notes.45:8: Unlike the Hebrew abstract nouns ("righteousness" and "salvation"), the Vulgate renders justum ("the Righteous One"), Salvatorem ("the Savior"), and eum ("Him") personally, giving this verse its classic messianic form; Latin germinet literally means "sprout" or "bud forth."
notes.45:24: Latin Ergo ("Therefore") and meæ sunt justitiæ et imperium ("my acts of righteousness and dominion") represent a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Hebrew reads "Only in the LORD, one shall say of me, are righteousness and strength."
notes.46:2: Latin Contabuerunt ("They have wasted away") and portantem ("the one carrying them") are Vulgate-distinct renderings where the Hebrew has "they stooped" and "the burden."
notes.46:3: The Vulgate uniquely includes first-person possessives in a meo utero ("from My belly") and a mea vulva ("from My womb"), whereas the Hebrew has "from the belly ... from the womb" without the pronoun.
notes.46:8: Latin confundamini ("be put to shame") differs from the Hebrew verb usually understood as "stand firm" or "take courage"; redite ... ad cor is literally "return to the heart," meaning to reflect earnestly.
notes.46:11: Latin avem renders the Hebrew "bird of prey" simply as "bird," and creavi ("I have created") translates a Hebrew verb meaning "I have formed" or "planned."
notes.47:2: Latin turpitudinem tuam ("your shame") and humerum ("shoulder") are distinctly Vulgate renderings where the Hebrew reads "your veil" and "skirt."
notes.47:3: Latin non resistet mihi homo ("no man will resist Me") differs from the Hebrew "I will not spare a man" (or "meet a man").
notes.47:8: Latin sterilitatem ("barrenness," and sterilitas in 47:9) translates a Hebrew noun meaning "bereavement" or "loss of children."
notes.47:11: Latin ortum ejus ("its rising") reflects a reading of the Hebrew term as "dawn/rising" rather than "charming it away."
notes.48:6: Latin "num annuntiastis?" expects a negative answer in the perfect tense ("have you declared them?") and repeats "ex tunc" ("from then", used throughout vv. 3, 5, 6, 7, 8), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "will you not declare it?" and "from now" here.
notes.48:9: Latin "laude mea infrenabo te" ("with My praise I will bridle you") makes Israel the direct object of God's restraint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of God restraining His anger for Israel's sake.
notes.48:10: Latin "elegi te in camino paupertatis" literally reads "I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty," preserving the primary sense of the Hebrew verb ("choose") and translating the noun as "poverty," whereas many translations from Hebrew render "tested you in the furnace of affliction."
notes.48:16: Latin "ex tempore antequam fieret" ("from the time before it came to be") emphasizes the speaker's preexistence before events unfolded, whereas the Hebrew reads "from the time it took place"; Christian interpretation traditionally identifies the speaker sent by "the Lord God ... and His Spirit" as the Messiah.
notes.49:5: Latin "et Israel non congregabitur" ("and Israel will not be gathered") follows the written Hebrew consonantal text (Ketiv, "not"), whereas most modern versions follow the marginal reading (Qere, "to Him": "that Israel might be gathered to Him").
notes.49:6: Latin "faeces Israel" literally reads "the dregs of Israel" (the remnant left at the bottom), differing from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "the preserved ones of Israel."
notes.49:9: Latin "in omnibus planis" ("on all the plains") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "on all the bare heights."
notes.49:12: Latin "de terra australi" ("from the southern land") translates geographically what the Hebrew Masoretic Text presents as a place name, "the land of Sinim."
notes.49:17: Latin "Venerunt structores tui" ("Your builders have come") reads the Hebrew consonants as "your builders" rather than the Masoretic Text's "your children," and renders the verb as "have come" rather than "hasten."
notes.50:2: Latin "Quia" ("For") introduces the verse as a declarative explanation of v. 1 rather than a question, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text opens with "Why?"
notes.50:4: Latin "ut audiam quasi magistrum" ("so that I may listen as to a master") uses the accusative "magistrum" as the object of hearing, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "to listen like those who are taught (disciples)."
notes.50:6: Latin "Corpus meum" ("my body") broadens the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "my back," and "ab increpantibus" ("from those who reproached me") uses a personal participle where the Hebrew has an abstract noun ("insults").
notes.50:11: Latin "in doloribus dormietis" literally reads "in sorrows you will sleep," rendering the Hebrew verb ("lie down") specifically as "sleep."
notes.51:3: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew place-name Eden according to its etymological meaning, delicias ('delights').
notes.51:5: The Vulgate renders justus meus ('My righteous one') and salvator meus ('My savior') as personal masculine nouns, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses the abstract nouns 'righteousness' and 'salvation.'
notes.51:9: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew name Rahab by its sense as superbum ('the proud one').
notes.51:14: Following the Latin strictly, the Vulgate speaks of one advancing swiftly to open who will not kill to utter destruction, whereas the Hebrew describes a crouching captive soon to be released who will not die in the pit.
notes.52:1: The Vulgate reads civitas Sancti ('city of the Holy One,' masculine singular genitive) rather than the Hebrew 'the holy city.'
notes.52:8: The Vulgate has the transitive verb converterit Dominus Sion ('when the Lord brings Zion back'), whereas the Hebrew reads 'when the Lord returns to Zion.'
notes.52:12: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew term for 'rearguard' literally from its verbal root as congregabit vos ('will gather you').
notes.52:14: The Vulgate reads inglorius ... inter viros ... inter filios hominum ('inglorious ... among men ... among the sons of men'), where the Hebrew describes his appearance as marred more than any man.
notes.52:15: The Vulgate reads quibus non est narratum de eo ('those to whom it has not been told about Him') with the perfect-tense verbs viderunt ('have seen') and contemplati sunt ('have contemplated'), diverging from the Hebrew future-tense 'what had not been told them they will see, and what they had not heard they will understand.'
notes.53:2: Latin et desideravimus eum is an affirmative indicative clause following non erat aspectus ("there was no appearance, and we desired him"), lacking the Hebrew negative/purpose sense "that we should desire him."
notes.53:4: The Vulgate uniquely renders Hebrew nagua ("stricken") as quasi leprosum ("like a leper").
notes.53:5: Latin livore is singular ("bruise" or "welt"), and scelera denotes grave crimes or wicked deeds.
notes.53:7: The Vulgate distinctly reads Oblatus est quia ipse voluit ("He was offered up because he himself willed it") rather than "He was oppressed and afflicted."
notes.53:8: Latin percussi eum is first-person singular ("I struck him") with God speaking, contrasting with third-person passive in Hebrew.
notes.53:9: Latin dabit is future tense ("he will give"), with singular divitem ("the rich man") for his death.
notes.53:12: Latin dispertiam ei plurimos ("I will allot to him very many") takes "very many" as the direct object rather than "with the many."
notes.54:1: Latin hinni literally means 'neigh,' Jerome's vivid rendering of the Hebrew verb tsahal, which conveys both the neighing of horses and a shrill shout of joy.
notes.54:9: The Vulgate reads in diebus Noe ('in the days of Noah') and cui juravi ('to whom I swore'), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text begins 'like the waters of Noah.'
notes.54:11: The Vulgate renders the setting of the stones as per ordinem ('in order') rather than Hebrew 'in antimony' (dark mortar), and in 54:12 reads jaspidem ('jasper') and lapides sculptos ('carved stones').
notes.54:15: Reading the Hebrew root in the sense of 'sojourning' rather than 'attacking,' the Vulgate turns this verse into a promise that a resident alien (accola) and former stranger (advena) will come and be joined to Zion.
notes.55:4: Vulgate praeceptorem means 'instructor' or 'teacher,' rendering the Hebrew term usually translated 'commander.'
notes.55:10: Vulgate inebriat terram, et infundit eam ('saturate the earth, and water it') differs from the Hebrew, which reads 'water the earth and make it bring forth.'
notes.55:13: Vulgate saliunca (wild spikenard, here used for a thorny brier) renders Hebrew na'atsuts ('thornbush'); erit Dominus nominatus ('the Lord will be renowned') makes 'the Lord' the subject rather than the dative 'to the Lord for a name' in the Hebrew.
notes.56:5: Vulgate locum ('a place') renders Hebrew yad (lit. 'hand,' often translated 'monument' or 'memorial').
notes.56:8: Vulgate congregabo ad eum congregatos ejus ('I will gather to him his gathered ones') takes 'his gathered ones' as the direct object, whereas the Hebrew reads 'besides those already gathered to him.'
notes.56:10: Vulgate videntes vana ('seeing empty things') and amantes somnia ('loving dreams') interpret Hebrew terms more commonly rendered 'dreaming/babbling' and 'loving to slumber.'
notes.56:11: Clementine Vulgate imprudentissimi ('most imprudent') is a variant of impudentissimi ('most shameless'), where the Hebrew reads 'strong of appetite' (greedy); a summo usque ad novissimum ('from the highest to the last') expands the Hebrew phrase meaning 'without exception.'
notes.57:5: Vulgate qui consolamini in diis ('who console yourselves in gods') diverges from the Hebrew, commonly translated 'who burn with lust among the oaks.'
notes.57:8: Vulgate juxta me ('beside Me'), suscepisti adulterum ('received an adulterer'), and manu aperta ('with an open hand') are distinct Vulgate readings differing from the Masoretic Text ('away from Me,' 'went up,' and 'looked on the hand/place').
notes.57:10: Vulgate Quiescam ('I will rest') and non rogasti ('you did not plead') differ from the Hebrew ('It is hopeless' and 'you did not grow faint'), while Vitam manus tuae ('the life of your hand') translates the Hebrew idiom for renewed strength literally.
notes.57:16: Vulgate egredietur ('will go out') and future faciam ('I will make') follow the Septuagint tradition rather than the Hebrew ('would grow faint' and past 'I have made').
notes.57:20: Vulgate in conculcationem ('into trampling') reflects Jerome's derivation of the Hebrew word for 'mire' (refesh) from the verb meaning 'to tread down.'
notes.58:3: Vulgate 'omnes debitores vestros repetitis' ("you demand payment from all your debtors") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which refers to oppressing all your workers.
notes.58:5: Vulgate 'contorquere quasi circulum caput suum' ("twist his head like a circle") renders the Hebrew word for "reed" or "bulrush" as a circle or hoop.
notes.58:11: Vulgate contains three distinctive readings here: 'requiem tibi dabit' ("give you rest," vs. Hebrew "guide you"), 'splendoribus' ("with splendors," vs. Hebrew "in scorched places"), and 'liberabit' ("deliver," vs. Hebrew "strengthen").
notes.58:12: Vulgate 'ædificator sepium, avertens semitas in quietem' ("builder of hedges, turning paths into quietness") diverges from the Hebrew, which reads "repairer of the breach, restorer of streets to dwell in."
notes.59:5: Vulgate 'quod confotum est, erumpet in regulum' ("what is warmed will burst forth into a basilisk") renders the Hebrew for a crushed egg as an incubated one and translates the serpent term with 'regulus' ("little king," i.e., basilisk).
notes.59:10: Vulgate 'in caliginosis' ("in gloomy places") interprets an obscure Hebrew word often rendered elsewhere as "among the vigorous" or "in desolate places."
notes.59:11: Vulgate 'quasi columbæ meditantes' ("like meditating doves") reflects the primary sense of the Hebrew verb 'hagah', which can mean either "to meditate" or "to murmur/coo."
notes.59:16: Vulgate 'aporiatus est' ("He was perplexed") borrows the Greek verb 'aporeo' ("to be at a loss") to translate the Hebrew verb for being appalled or astonished.
notes.60:1: Vulgate 'illuminare' is a passive imperative ("be illumined"), differing from the active imperative ("shine") in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.60:4: Vulgate 'de latere surgent' ("will rise from the side") diverges from the Hebrew, which describes daughters being carried on the hip or side.
notes.60:9: Vulgate 'naves maris' ("ships of the sea") follows Jerome's frequent rendering of "Tarshish" as "the sea" in Isaiah, and uses the first-person verb 'adducam' ("I may bring").
notes.60:17: Vulgate 'visitationem tuam' ("your visitation," i.e., oversight) translates the Hebrew noun commonly rendered "your overseers" or "your governance."
notes.60:18: Vulgate 'occupabit salus muros tuos' ("salvation will occupy your walls") differs from the Hebrew, which reads "you shall call your walls Salvation."
notes.61:1: Vulgate reads "the Spirit of the Lord" (without "God" as in the Hebrew), "heal" (mederer) rather than Hebrew "bind up," "pardon" (indulgentiam, a legal term for amnesty or remission), and literally "opening to those confined" (clausis apertionem), preserving the ambiguity between opening a prison and opening eyes.
notes.61:3: Vulgate uniquely includes "in her" (in ea, referring to Zion) and renders the Hebrew term often translated "oaks" or "terebinths" as "mighty ones" (fortes justitiae), concluding with the gerund "for glorification" (ad glorificandum).
notes.61:7: Vulgate connects "double" (duplici) to "your shame" ("Instead of your double shame and disgrace"), whereas the Hebrew text reads "Instead of your shame, a double portion."
notes.61:8: Vulgate reads "robbery in a burnt offering" (rapinam in holocausto), interpreting the Hebrew noun as "burnt offering" rather than "wrongdoing," and translates the following term literally as "their work" (opus eorum) rather than "recompense."
notes.62:1: Instead of the abstract Hebrew nouns "her righteousness" and "her salvation," Vulgate uses personal masculine nouns here ("her righteous one," "her savior") and in 62:2 ("your righteous one," "your renowned one"), and uses the passive verb "is kindled" (accendatur).
notes.62:4: Vulgate translates rather than transliterates the Hebrew symbolic names, rendering Hephzibah ("My delight is in her") as "My Will Is in Her" (Voluntas mea in ea) and Beulah ("Married") as "Inhabited" (Inhabitata), continuing with "will dwell" (habitabit/habitabunt) rather than "marry" in 62:5.
notes.62:8: Latin preserves the elliptical biblical oath formula literally ("If I again give your wheat... and if foreign sons drink your wine..."), which expresses an emphatic negation ("Never again will I give...").
notes.62:12: Following the Clementine Vulgate punctuation (Quaesita civitas, et non Derelicta), "City" is grouped with "Sought-Out" rather than with "Not Abandoned" as in the Hebrew text.
notes.63:6: Vulgate translates the final noun as "their strength" (virtutem eorum), whereas many modern translations of the Hebrew understand a homonymous root meaning "their lifeblood."
notes.63:9: Following the Hebrew Ketiv ("not") against the Qere ("to Him"), Vulgate explicitly reads "He was not afflicted" (non est tribulatus), and renders the following title literally as "the angel of His face" (angelus faciei ejus).
notes.63:10: Both here (spiritum Sancti ejus) and in 63:11 (spiritum Sancti sui), the Clementine Vulgate uses the capitalized genitive singular "of His Holy One" rather than an adjective agreeing with "Spirit" ("His Holy Spirit").
notes.63:12: Vulgate makes Moses the direct object of "led out" ("who led Moses out at the right hand by the arm of His majesty") rather than the Hebrew "who caused His glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moses"; similarly in 63:14, Vulgate follows the Septuagint with "was its leader" (ductor ejus fuit) rather than Hebrew "gave them rest."
notes.63:18: Vulgate reads "As nothing they have possessed Your holy people" (Quasi nihilum possederunt populum sanctum tuum), making the adversaries the subject and Your holy people the object, whereas the Hebrew is commonly translated "For a little while Your holy people possessed it."
notes.64:1: In the Vulgate chapter division, 64:1 continues the sentence begun in 63:19 about the mountains melting at God's presence; Latin also reads "burning of fire" (exustio ignis) and "would burn" (arderent), where the Hebrew refers to kindling brushwood and making water boil.
notes.64:2: Vulgate uses future tenses ("When You do ... we will not endure," Cum feceris ... non sustinebimus) rather than the Hebrew past ("when you did awesome things we did not expect"); Latin sustineo can mean either "endure" or "wait for."
notes.64:4: Vulgate reads an indicative statement of hope, "and we will be saved" (et salvabimur), where the Hebrew clause is grammatically difficult and often translated as a question ("shall we be saved?").
notes.64:6: Vulgate reads allisisti ("crushed" or "dashed down"), whereas the Hebrew reads "melted us" (or "delivered us into the hand of our iniquities").
notes.64:9: Vulgate reads singular Civitas Sancti tui ("The city of Your Holy One," which can also be taken as "of Your sanctuary"), whereas the Hebrew has plural "Your holy cities."
notes.65:1: Vulgate uses active verbs ("have sought Me ... have found [Me]," Quæsierunt me ... invenerunt), whereas the Hebrew and Septuagint (cf. Rom 10:20) use passive forms ("I was sought ... I was found").
notes.65:5: Vulgate reads "because you are unclean" (quia immundus es), contrasting with the Hebrew ("for I am too holy for you").
notes.65:11: Vulgate renders Hebrew Gad as "Fortune" (fortunæ) and omits the second pagan deity name (Hebrew Meni, "Destiny"), reading instead "pour drink offerings on it" (super eam, referring to the table).
notes.65:16: Vulgate transliterates the Hebrew title "God of truth" (Elohei amen) directly as "in God, amen" (in Deo, amen).
notes.65:22: Vulgate places "My chosen ones" (Electi mei) at the start of verse 23 and makes "the works of their hands" the subject of inveterabunt ("will grow old," i.e., endure to great age), unlike the Hebrew ("my chosen will long enjoy the work of their hands").
notes.65:25: Vulgate reads "the lion and the ox" (leo et bos), whereas the Hebrew reads "the lion like the ox."
notes.66:3: Vulgate excerebret ("dashes out the brains of") differs from the Hebrew ("breaks the neck of"), and recordatur thuris ("remembers frankincense") literally renders the Hebrew idiom for making a memorial offering of frankincense.
notes.66:6: Vulgate reads "The voice of the people" (Vox populi), whereas the Hebrew reads "A sound of uproar."
notes.66:17: Vulgate reads "behind the door inside" (post januam intrinsecus), whereas the Hebrew reads "following one in the center."
notes.66:18: Vulgate resolves the broken Hebrew syntax by making "their works and their thoughts" the direct object of "to gather" (ut congregem), alongside "all nations and tongues."
notes.66:19: Vulgate identifies the Hebrew names Tarshish, Pul, Lud, Tubal, and Javan as "the sea" (mare), "Africa," "Lydia," "Italy," and "Greece," and reads "aiming the arrow" (tendentes sagittam) where the Hebrew has "drawing the bow."
notes.66:24: Vulgate renders the rare Hebrew term deraon ("abhorrence") etymologically as usque ad satietatem visionis ("even to satiety of sight"), conveying being sated to disgust at the sight.

unplaced.text: Therefore, cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, because he himself has been considered exalted.
unplaced.note: The Latin Vulgate reads a declarative statement here (quia excelsus reputatus est ipse, "because he himself has been considered exalted"), unlike the Hebrew rhetorical question ("of what account is he?").

unplaced.text: "Come, let us get wine, and let us be filled with drunkenness; and just as it is today, so it will also be tomorrow, and much more."
unplaced.note: The Latin presents the shepherds' boast directly without an introductory verb and reads plural sumamus ("let us get") with ebrietate ("drunkenness").
